# Counted Complexity Assertions

Turning an asymptotic claim into an ordinary unit-test assertion by **counting operations
instead of measuring time**.

## The problem with the obvious approach

A test that asserts merge sort beats insertion sort by the clock is a test about the machine
it ran on. It passes on a quiet laptop, fails on a loaded CI runner, and in neither case says
anything about the algorithms. So complexity claims end up in comments, where nothing checks
them and they drift away from the code underneath.

## The mechanism

1. **Charge the algorithm.** Every operation takes a counter and increments it for each key
   comparison, element move and structural probe. The cost becomes part of the signature, not
   an estimate made afterwards.
2. **Measure over a doubling series.** Run at `n, 2n, 4n, …` with a fresh counter each time.
3. **Fit scale-free.** For each candidate growth function `g`, take the constant that best
   explains the data — the mean of `ops(n) / g(n)` — and score the candidate by mean relative
   error. Lowest wins. Dividing the constant out is what makes the verdict an *order* and
   nothing else, which is exactly the claim asymptotic notation makes.
4. **Assert the class.** `assertEquals(Growth.LINEARITHMIC, classify(measure(sizes, work)))`.

Counts are deterministic for a fixed input, so the assertion is reproducible everywhere. The
same idea appears in a different guise in [[cryptanalysis-by-measurement]]: replace an
argument about behaviour with a number the code produces.

## What it is not

**Not a proof.** It measures the sizes it was given over the inputs it was given. A quadratic
worst case hiding behind a linear average is a property of the input generator, which is why
a quicksort test that wants to see the worst case must feed it a sorted array on purpose.

**Not able to name a class outside its candidate set.** Shell sort is `O(n^1.5)` and jump
search `O(√n)`; with neither in the candidates, both are asserted negatively — "not
quadratic", "the cost doubles when `n` quadruples" — rather than forced into a box. An honest
negative beats a confident wrong label.

**Not immune to small `n`.** `n/4 + 1000` classifies as constant at `n ≤ 512` and linear at
`n ≥ 8192`, and the fitter is correct both times: asymptotic behaviour is a claim about large
`n`. Every growth assertion has to pick sizes where the term under test dominates, and the
disagreement itself is worth keeping as a test.

## What it caught

Two documented claims that were wrong, found because the measurement disagreed with the
javadoc:

- **Repeated heap insertion measures linear on shuffled input.** The familiar `O(n log n)` is
  the worst case; a random key sifts up about one level. The gap appears only on descending
  keys.
- **Linear probing with nearly consecutive hashes is not constant per operation at all.** Its
  measured total is neither linear nor monotonic in `n`, while double hashing on the same keys
  is a straight line.

Both were fixed in the documentation rather than by relaxing the assertion, which is the
useful direction: see [[document-the-failure-mode-next-to-the-fix]] and
[[data-structures-and-algorithms]] for the full record.
